Getting out is the harder problem: throttling new admissions recovered 1 of 7 matched collapsed runs, while suspending admitted sessions against a capacity-based limit recovered all of them within minutes. A CPU offload tier delays the collapse but does not prevent it. A budgeter that bounds the resident KV demand of active sessions to the pool, with thresholds that need no per-workload tuning, prevented the failure in every run we tested.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 12 pages, 8 figures

Hardware Architecture.title: Plumbline: When the Loss Lies, Validating LLM Training Correctly
Hardware Architecture.summary: Correctness is a prerequisite for training large language models (LLMs) at scale, yet it is hard to ensure: a fault can sit in any part of a run, and how it shows differs across frameworks and the libraries they depend on. Some failures are loud and some are silent, and both take time to detect and trace. A single fault can waste a long run: the run crashes late, or the model scores lower only at the final evaluation. We present Plumbline, a correctness validation system for LLM training, used in production at Amazon. Plumbline checks each part of the training lifecycle, from the data a run trains on to the model it serves, down to the new layers each model brings and up to whole runs. Its diagnosis reuses these checks to trace failures to their root causes. Both rest on a systematic correctness methodology designed to carry across models and frameworks. Plumbline supports two agentic use cases: Day-0 onboarding, which validates the training of a newly released model before teams rely on it, and root-cause tracing of training failures. Across 3 frameworks and 5 models, it found 61 problems, 32 of them silent. Of these, 42 are fixed or reported upstream, 8 of them first raised by us. We further group the 61 into seven failure patterns that show where training breaks, and report how problems recur across frameworks and models.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 16 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables

Hardware Architecture.title: MARS: Towards High Goodput and Low KV Thrashing in Agent Serving under GPU Memory Constraints
Hardware Architecture.summary:
Self-hosted LLM agents offer greater control over sensitive data and model customization while avoiding per-request API fees. However, serving concurrent, multi-turn workflows within limited GPU memory makes it difficult to achieve high workflow-level goodput. In particular, as workflows accumulate context, their reusable key-value (KV) caches can easily outgrow GPU capacity, triggering repeated eviction and recovery, known as KV cache thrashing. This process consumes resources and delays workflow completion. Although existing approaches propose various methods, our motivation study shows that the evaluated baselines still incur substantial thrashing overhead or fail to address the workflow-level goodput issue.
  We present MARS, an agent serving system that coordinates workflow admission and in-engine scheduling to achieve high workflow-level goodput on memory-constrained devices while avoiding KV cache thrashing. Specifically, outside the engine, an admission controller selects root workflows using initial prefix footprint estimates and live KV availability, adapting admissions to memory pressure. Inside, an agent-centric scheduler prioritizes turn completion and coordinates prefill allocation with KV reclamation to reduce disruptive evictions. Across two models and three GPU configurations, MARS achieves 1.59x-7.56x mean end-to-end latency speedups over the fastest baseline. Integrated as the serving backend for OpenCode, Codex, and OpenHands, MARS further improves mean workflow completion time by 1.17x-1.87x.
  Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Afterglow231/MARS_preview .
Hardware Architecture.comment: 13 pages, 11 figures. Major revision with updated title, system design, and expanded evaluation. Preprint

Hardware Architecture.title: Mean field optimal Core Allocation across Malleable jobs
Hardware Architecture.summary:
Modern data centers and cloud computing clusters are increasingly running workloads composed of malleable jobs. A malleable job can be parallelized across any number of cores, yet the job typically exhibits diminishing marginal returns for each additional core on which it runs. Examples of malleable jobs include machine learning tasks, parallelized across multiple GPUs, and large-scale database queries, parallelized across multiple servers.
  Given the prevalence of malleable jobs, theoretical works have posed the problem of how to allocate a fixed number of cores across a stream of arriving malleable jobs so as to minimize the mean response time across jobs. We refer to this as the Core Allocation to Malleable jobs (CAM) problem. Although quite a few recent papers have been written on CAM, the problem remains challenging to solve optimally. In particular, prior theoretical work has only solved the CAM problem in very constrained cases.
  This paper takes a new approach to CAM, looking at the problem in the mean field asymptotic regime. In this regime, we are able to optimally solve a much more general instance of CAM. We derive two distinct mean field optimal policies, FW-CAM and GLAM. FW-CAM demonstrates a new intuition: in the mean field regime, individual job sizes are not relevant in finding an optimal policy. GLAM (Gittins-Like Allocation for Malleable jobs) is asymptotically optimal under certain common assumptions, and also serves as a good heuristic outside of the asymptotic regime by adapting dynamically to the current number of jobs in the system. Notably, none of the policies previously proposed in the literature are mean field optimal when jobs follow different speedup functions.

Hardware Architecture.title: BOA Constrictor: Squeezing Performance out of GPUs in the Cloud via Budget-Optimal Allocation
Hardware Architecture.summary:
The past decade has seen a dramatic increase in demand for GPUs to train Machine Learning (ML) models. Because it is prohibitively expensive for most organizations to build and maintain a large GPU cluster, organizations instead choose to rent GPUs from cloud providers. The customer is responsible for devising a policy for (i) deciding how many GPUs to rent at every moment in time to process a stream of ML training jobs and (ii) allocating the rented GPUs among the currently active jobs in the system. Because ML training jobs can be parallelized across different numbers of GPUs, the customer generally has many options for how many GPUs to use for each job. Allocating more GPUs to a single training job will cause the job to complete more quickly. However, the customer pays for each GPU-hour they use, and a training job receives a diminishing marginal benefit from running on additional GPUs. Hence, allocating too many GPUs to a single training job can dramatically increase the overall cost that the customer pays to the cloud provider. This gives rise to a cost-performance tradeoff that customers must balance when running training jobs in the cloud.
  To balance the cost-performance tradeoff, we develop BOA Constrictor, a new scheduler for ML training jobs which uses a Budget-Optimal Allocation (BOA) policy to squeeze the highest level of performance out of a cloud-deployed GPU cluster given a fixed budget constraint. We explicitly formulate the problem as a budget-constrained scheduling problem and derive the BOA policy which minimizes the average job completion time (JCT) of a stream of arriving jobs subject to the user's budget. For a given budget level, we demonstrate that BOA Constrictor can reduce average JCT by 1.6 times in small-scale implementation experiments and by 2 times in detailed, large-scale simulations compared to state-of-the-art heuristic based schedulers.

Hardware Architecture.title: Hybrid FedGraph: An efficient hybrid federated learning algorithm using graph convolutional neural network
Hardware Architecture.summary: Federated learning is an emerging paradigm for decentralized training of machine learning models on distributed clients, without revealing the data to the central server. Most existing works have focused on horizontal or vertical data distributions, where each client possesses different samples with shared features, or each client fully shares only sample indices, respectively. However, the hybrid scheme is much less studied, even though it is much more common in the real world. Therefore, in this paper, we propose a generalized algorithm, FedGraph, that introduces a graph convolutional neural network to capture feature-sharing information while learning features from a subset of clients. We also develop a simple but effective clustering algorithm that aggregates features produced by the deep neural networks of each client while preserving data privacy.
Hardware Architecture.comment: This preliminary version was evaluated only in a vertical setting on one dataset, its clustering exposes labels to the server, and it has been superseded by a substantially revised approach. It has no standalone value.

Hardware Architecture.title: OSCAR: Offline Spectral Covariance-Aware Rotation for 2-bit KV Cache Quantization
Hardware Architecture.summary:
INT2 KV-cache quantization is attractive for long-context LLM serving, yet making it both accurate and practical remains challenging. Data-oblivious rotations such as Hadamard transforms flatten channel outliers, but still degrade sharply at INT2 because they ignore how downstream attention queries the cache. We propose OSCAR, an ultra-low-bit KV-cache quantization method that estimates attention-aware covariance targets offline and uses them to derive fixed per-layer rotations and clipping thresholds. By aligning the quantization basis with the second-moment structures consumed by attention, OSCAR preserves attention fidelity at 2-bit precision. Beyond theoretical analysis under a frozen-error surrogate, we build a serving-ready OSCAR system with fused Triton write and decode kernels that preserve paged KV-cache layouts and prefix caching, integrating into modern serving engines such as SGLang and vLLM.
  We evaluate OSCAR on reasoning and coding benchmarks with generation traces of up to 32K tokens across five tasks. On Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and Qwen3-8B, OSCAR narrows the BF16 accuracy gap to 3.78 and 1.21 points, respectively, where Hadamard-only INT2 collapses, and matches BF16 within run-to-run variance on Qwen3-32B and GLM-4.7 (358B parameters). On RULER-NIAH up to 128K tokens, OSCAR substantially outperforms QuaRot-style INT2 across context lengths. System-wise, OSCAR compresses KV-cache memory by nearly $8\times$, boosts multi-request throughput by up to $7.8\times$ at large batch sizes within the same memory budget, and accelerates batch-size-1 decoding by up to $3.1\times$ over BF16 by cutting KV memory traffic.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 46 pages, 10 figures. v2 adds matched-baseline comparisons, residual diagnostics, and expanded long-context analysis

Hardware Architecture.title: HAWK: Heterogeneity-Aware KV Cache Transfer for Efficient GPU-NPU Phase-Disaggregated LLM Inference
Hardware Architecture.summary:
Large language model (LLM) inference exhibits distinct computational characteristics across its two phases: prefill is compute-intensive, whereas decode is more memory-bound. As a result, AI accelerators achieve varying levels of efficiency across the two phases. GPUs are well suited to prefill, but are often underutilized during decode. By contrast, NPUs can utilize their compute resources more effectively during decode. Motivated by this observation, we explore a heterogeneous architecture that integrates GPUs and NPUs, mapping prefill to GPUs and decode to NPUs to achieve high performance and efficiency. However, realizing such heterogeneous integration is challenging because LLM phase disaggregation requires KV cache transfer from prefill to decode (that is, from GPUs to NPUs), which is complicated by differences in inter-device communication mechanisms and KV cache tensor layouts.
  To address this, we propose HAWK, a transfer mechanism that enables rapid KV cache transfer across heterogeneous devices. HAWK establishes a remote direct memory access (RDMA) path for direct cross-device transfers while handling inter-device tensor layout discrepancies as part of the transfer process. In particular, HAWK allocates tensor-layout-aware RDMA buffers on the NPU side to match the target tensor layout. Leveraging these buffers, HAWK orchestrates data transfer from a conventional contiguous GPU RDMA buffer to the corresponding NPU buffers, allowing transferred tensors to be consumed directly without additional data rearrangement while maintaining transfer efficiency. We implement and evaluate HAWK on a system built with commercially available GPUs and NPUs, demonstrating performance within 7.88% of a GPU-only system under the same SLO constraints while achieving up to 1.26$\times$ higher power efficiency and 1.72$\times$ higher cost efficiency.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 15 pages, 14 figures, 9 tables

Hardware Architecture.title: SlipStream: Enabling HBF for GPU Systems by Mitigating the Latency and SRAM Overheads
Hardware Architecture.summary:
Large language model (LLM) inference demands ever more memory capacity for larger models and batch sizes. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) replaces the DRAM dies of HBM with NAND flash and provides up to 16x the capacity at comparable read bandwidth. However, HBF can incur a read latency of nearly 20$μ$s, 20x that of HBM, so on-demand HBF accesses slow inference by up to 12.8x. Conventional cache-line prefetchers require 20x more in-flight tracking state to cover this latency. Tensor-streaming designs, such as H3, follow virtual-address order as opposed to kernel-demand order, and therefore need hundreds of megabytes of buffering.
  We propose SlipStream, a software-hardware co-designed prefetcher that turns prefetching into a demand-paced producer-consumer pipeline. In software, SlipStream profiles the repeatable weight-page demand order of data-independent LLM kernels and inserts a staging warp that replays this order with non-blocking STAGE instructions. In hardware, the staging warp acts as the producer and the work warps as consumers. Our key insight is to retire each STAGE tracking entry only when demand first accesses the page, as opposed to when the page returns from HBF. Demand thus paces staging and bounds how far staging leads consumption. SlipStream tracks 4 KB pages instead of cache lines and allocates buffer slots only when pages return, which decouples the buffer size from outstanding traffic. Across seven dense models spanning 16-800 GB, SlipStream with a 40 MB staging buffer achieves 92.4% of the performance of an ideal HBF with HBM-like latency. H3 achieves only 43.1%, even with a 320 MB buffer. The buffer sizing of SlipStream is independent of HBF latency and workload. SlipStream with 16 MB buffer, 20x smaller than that of H3, performs within 4% of SlipStream-40MB. SlipStream also supports Mixture-of-Experts models and reaches 91.2% of ideal performance (40 MB buffer).
Hardware Architecture.comment: To appear in 2027 IEEE International Symposium on High-Performance Computer Architecture (HPCA)

Hardware Architecture.title: Toward Optimal-Complexity Hash-Based Asynchronous MVBA with Optimal Resilience
Hardware Architecture.summary:
Multi-valued validated Byzantine agreement (MVBA), a fundamental primitive of distributed computing, allows $n$ processes to agree on a valid $\ell$-bit value, despite $t$ faulty processes behaving maliciously. Among hash-based solutions for the asynchronous setting with adaptive faults, the state-of-the-art HMVBA protocol achieves optimal $O(n^2)$ message complexity, (near-)optimal $O(n \ell + n^2 λ\log n)$ bit complexity, and optimal $O(1)$ time complexity. However, it only tolerates $t < \frac15 n$ failures. In contrast, the best-known optimally-resilient protocol, SQ, incurs a higher bit complexity of $O(n^2 \ell + n^3 λ)$. This poses a fundamental question: Can a hash-based protocol be designed for the asynchronous setting with adaptive faults that simultaneously achieves optimal complexity and optimal resilience?
  This paper takes a significant step toward answering this question. Namely, we introduce Reducer, an MVBA protocol that retains HMVBA's optimal complexity while improving its resilience to $t < \frac14 n$. Like HMVBA and SQ, Reducer relies exclusively on collision-resistant hash functions. A key innovation in Reducer's design is its internal use of strong multi-valued Byzantine agreement (SMBA), a new variant of Byzantine agreement we introduce and construct, which ensures that the decided value was proposed by a correct process. To further advance resilience toward the optimal one-third bound, we then propose Reducer++, an MVBA protocol that tolerates up to $t < (\frac13 - ε)n$ adaptive failures, for any fixed constant $ε> 0$. Unlike Reducer, Reducer++ does not rely on SMBA. Instead, it employs a novel approach involving hash functions modeled as random oracles to ensure termination. Reducer++ maintains constant time complexity, quadratic message complexity, and quasi-quadratic bit complexity, with constants dependent on $ε$.

Hardware Architecture.title: Reconstructing Fine-grained Memory Reuse Structure in GPU Kernels
Hardware Architecture.summary: Optimizing GPU data movement requires knowing which instructions access the same data and across which execution scopes reuse occurs. Existing profilers can attribute memory behavior to individual instructions but do not expose the reuse relations among them, while aliasing, dynamic indexing, and runtime parameters prevent static analysis from establishing these relations in general. Cycle-level simulation can reconstruct such relations, but at costs prohibitive for production workloads. We introduce two abstractions for representing this structure: Topological Distance, which labels each dynamic memory access with the smallest execution scope (thread, warp, block, or grid) containing its most recent reuse, and PCDepGraph, which organizes these labels into a PC-level graph of the kernel's memory reuse structure. Defined over logical execution scopes rather than transient hardware state, the representation remains stable across runs and GPU targets while directly indicating the sharing scope that candidate optimization mechanisms must cover. Our tool, cuVein, reconstructs PCDepGraph directly from optimized binaries, without sampling, at generally under 10x overhead. Across HPC and AI workloads on NVIDIA RTX 4090 and H100, optimizations guided by PCDepGraph eliminate up to 90.18% of memory instructions and yield up to 2.84x kernel speedup; reuse-scope distributions remain consistent across platforms, supporting that the representation captures program structure rather than transient hardware behavior.

Databases.title: MammothDP: Private Boosted Decision Trees Ready for Trusted Hardware and Leakage-free Hyperparameters
Databases.summary: Data spaces like the European Health Data Space (EHDS) require the protection of sensitive data in studies during the data's processing and the study's release alike. In this work, we investigate how to implement this mandate using established trusted execution environments (TEEs) and timing side-channel hardening to protect the processing even under a compromised server, and the state-of-the-art differential privacy (DP) notion to protect the release of studies on tabular data. This combined setup could seem to complete the picture, but in fact raises unexpected security challenges that we mitigate by introducing MammothDP: a significant milestone towards a holistic machine learning system based on the recent gradient boosted decision tree learner S-BDT that is provably DP if used within a privacy filter, timing side-channel hardened, and deployed on a TEE. To achieve a strong privacy-utility tradeoff, we introduce two novel components: an early stopping criterion that adaptively selects the number of trees without any privacy overhead, and an improved rollback protection that is no longer vulnerable under timing side-channel attacks.

Databases.title: Measuring Tabular Data Formats Cold: A Replicated Cold-Cache Benchmark of Serialization, Scan, and Index Performance on Real Datasets
Databases.summary: Choosing a file format for tabular data is a routine engineering decision, yet published comparisons often time reads served from the operating-system page cache, use one session, or rely on a single synthetic dataset. This article benchmarks fifteen format and access-path configurations (CSV, JSON Lines, Pickle, Feather, Parquet, ORC, DuckDB, and SQLite, with several access paths) on two real public datasets, New York City taxi trips and United States airline on-time records, at 50,000 to 3 million rows. Every measurement uses an explicitly cold cache, randomized execution order, and three independent sessions (with restarts on the laptop), and is analyzed with bootstrap intervals and Holm-adjusted permutation tests. Parquet answered a filtered aggregation 2.6 to 11 times faster than CSV, while JSON Lines was 10 to 27 times slower. A secondary index made SQLite queries 2.6 to 4.8 times slower on randomly ordered data and helped only on data sorted by the filtered column, at low selectivity. A row filter inside the Parquet reader was significantly faster than a projected scan on flight data from one million rows and on both datasets at three million, and row-group skipping needs several row groups, which the default writer produced only at 3 million rows. A 4 GB Linux host ran out of memory on configurations that a 24 GB laptop completed and reversed some orderings, such as Pickle versus Parquet. Code, derived data, and raw timings are released.
Databases.comment: Submitted to IEEE Open Journal of the Computer Society

Databases.title: Selective Retrieval Routing for Multi-Violation Knowledge Graph Repair
Databases.summary: Knowledge graphs often contain missing or inconsistent facts that undermine the applications built on them. Schema validation detects such violations but does not identify which of several valid repairs recovers the intended graph. External corpora can supply the evidence needed to identify the intended repair, but retrieving from them is costly and not always successful. We propose a framework for selective retrieval in iterative graph repair. An LLM repair agent explores and edits the graph, while a router controls its access to a researcher agent that retrieves external evidence. We extend a violation-injection framework to generate cases with multiple compatible violations and known reference repairs. The agent's repair outcomes on these cases provide supervision for training the deployment-specific router. On two building-automation datasets, researcher access improves repairs for some violations and degrades them for others, with effects differing across deployments. The router uses fewer repair-time tokens than always enabling access in all six evaluation suites. It achieves higher repair $F_1$ than always disabling access in five of six suites.

Databases.title: Fairness-Aware Retrieval Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Databases.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds large language models (LLMs) in external knowledge, but the retrieved documents can systematically skew generated answers toward one group. This effect is difficult to analyze and control in top-k settings, where several documents at different context positions jointly shape the output. We present a three-stage framework for fairness-aware retrieval in top-k RAG. First, a probabilistic reranker sets the group composition of the retrieved context at each position, enabling controlled perturbation of retrieval bias without modifying the retriever. Second, we show that output bias is well approximated by a position-weighted linear function of position-wise retrieval bias, revealing model-specific positional sensitivities. Third, we use this model to formulate retrieval as an optimization problem that trades off relevance against predicted output bias, and propose FARO, a scalable solution to that problem which decomposes the globally coupled quadratic objective into independent per-query assignment problems through a Fenchel--Legendre dual reformulation. Experiments with four open LLMs, and political and gender bias as use cases show that the linear model predicts output bias on unseen configurations in 17 of 24 settings. FARO substantially reduces output bias in most settings, while, compared with a linear-programming baseline, FARO achieves similar relevance, remains feasible where the baseline does not, and scales better to larger query sets and candidate pools.

Databases.title: Messier: A High-Resolution Corpus for Cross-Benchmark Agent Evaluation
Databases.summary: Comprehensively evaluating AI agents across interactive environments is difficult due to fragmented tasks, scaffolds, verifiers, and scoring rules. Unfortunately, existing efforts to unify these evaluations are limited in scale and domain, making costly reruns necessary and leaving available data incomparable. We introduce Messier, a unified corpus of 923,158 records spanning 30 benchmarks, 745 agents, 11,891 tasks, and 71,969 verifiers. Messier combines public evaluation results with new runs on six underrepresented professional and scientific benchmarks, standardizing their heterogeneous components into a common schema. Using this corpus, we show that frontier progress is uneven across benchmark groups, with function-calling evaluations largely saturated, programming improving fastest, and enterprise workflows remaining most challenging. Counterfactual rescoring further shows that reported performance can be highly sensitive to how verifier results are aggregated. Finally, we derive capability scores from our corpus that correlate with Epoch's Evaluation Capability Index rankings at Spearman \r{ho} = 0.84. The scores can also be estimated for subsets defined by domain, occupation, action space, or verifier type. In essence, Messier is a reusable resource for studying agent performance at scale, and a basis for designing better evaluations.

Databases.title: SAIL: Self-Adaptive Index Learning with Hybrid Models (Extended Version)
Databases.summary: Learned index structures have demonstrated a significant improvement in query performance over traditional index structures. The majority of learned indexes use a uniform node structure throughout their index structures. A few studies show that combining multiple types of node structures can lead to indexes that better adapt to local key-set distributions, hence yielding query efficiency gains. Following this line of work, we propose a learned index structure named SAIL that supports a wide range of different candidate node structures for both leaf and inner nodes, selected via cost models based on data driven approximations. We design an efficient construction algorithm that recursively partitions the key-set to be fitted by the candidate node types. Experiments demonstrate that SAIL achieves 2x improvement over existing learned indexes in query time, with similar memory consumption and index build times.

Databases.title: PLDP-IDS: Personalized Local Differential Privacy for Infinite Data Stream
Databases.summary: Streaming data collection under local differential privacy (LDP) enables real-time analytics without a trusted curator. Existing w-event LDP mechanisms, however, impose a uniform privacy window and budget on all users, forcing everyone to adopt the most stringent requirement. We study personalized continual frequency estimation under LDP, where each user specifies her own window size and privacy budget, and identify two challenges. First, a single sampling size cannot balance sampling and perturbation errors for privacy groups with heterogeneous requirements. Second, borrowing estimates from groups with larger budgets reduces variance but introduces bias when privacy preferences correlate with the data. We first propose Optimal Population Selection (OPS) and two OPS-guided mechanisms, PLPD and PLPA. We then develop PLPD+ and PLPA+, which combine group-aware population scheduling with bias-aware cross-group fusion while preserving personalized w-event LDP. Experiments on real-world and synthetic streams show that PLPA+ reduces the AMSE of the direct personalized extension of LDP-IDS by 52.3% and 40.8% on average, respectively, and remains about $5\times$ more accurate than PLPA under strong privacy--data correlation.

Databases.title: Beyond Interaction Scores: Selecting Feature Interactions via Independent Replication
Databases.summary: Learning feature interactions is essential for accurate prediction and interpretable modeling, yet a high interaction score may reflect fitting noise rather than a reproducible pattern. Ranking methods score feature pairs but leave the cutoff to the user; testing methods set the cutoff but rely on repeated model refits or a model of the joint feature distribution. We present LENS, a model-agnostic framework for selecting feature interactions through independent replication. LENS trains two models with the same learning algorithm on disjoint data and accesses them only through predictions. For each feature pair, it removes main effects from the joint-effect surface to isolate an interaction pattern, ranks pairs by its strength, and tests whether the second model reproduces it at a meaningful strength. A single multiple-testing correction determines which pairs to retain, using only two model fits regardless of the number of features. We prove that a replication ratio alone can retain arbitrarily weak patterns shared by both fits, whereas a strength floor restores selection consistency, and we characterize when normalization in Friedman's $H^2$ reverses interaction rankings. On 16 synthetic designs, LENS matches leading model-specific ranking methods (e.g., TreeSHAP) and recovers 91% of material interactions, against 45% for the knockoff-based DIAMOND, without selecting false pairs; with 1,225 candidate pairs and no interactions, it makes substantially fewer false discoveries. On large-scale French motor insurance data, it identifies interactions documented in the actuarial literature and recovers 90% of the deviance gain obtained using all pairs. On two credit datasets, LENS selects few pairs while maintaining or slightly improving predictive performance over the additive baseline.
Databases.comment: 20 pages. Code and results: https://github.com/JinchengGao-Infty/LENS

Databases.title: SynthCorp: A Platform for Creating Benchmarks for Data Agents
Databases.summary: Current benchmarks for LLM-driven data agents saturate quickly and cannot target specific capabilities. We present SynthCorp, a platform that creates customizable data estates and benchmarks by simulating how business events produce and modify corporate data over time. Each data estate combines relational databases, a document store, and a data catalog, paired with evaluation tasks and executable gold programs. First, given a scenario and target complexity dimensions, SynthCorp synthesizes reusable event types and compiles each into a program over predefined simulation primitives. Second, SynthCorp schedules event instances on a virtual calendar, interleaving routine and disruption events so that tables, documents, and catalog entries remain consistent. Third, SynthCorp executes the calendar to materialize the data estate and records every operation in a simulation log. Fourth, SynthCorp generates analytical tasks and derives verified gold programs from the log. We use SynthCorp to generate initial evaluation benchmarks comprising seven data estates (up to 1K operational tables) and 256 tasks across five domains. The data estates pass deterministic pipeline checks (such as foreign-key violations, undeclared writes, recurrence violations, and database execution failures) with a near-zero error rate, introduce cross-asset complexities, and cover all requested dimensions. Evaluating three models across four data-context settings shows that the benchmarks separate data contexts and model tiers. Auditing candidate queries against causal provenance in the simulation log verifies gold programs without manual annotation, including on multi-event composite tasks that expose reasoning failures in state-of-the-art agents. We hope the community uses SynthCorp to generate more challenging and useful data estates and benchmarks that foster the development of enterprise data agents.
Databases.comment: SynthCorp v1.0. We will release the benchmarks soon

Databases.title: HistogramTools for Efficient Data Analysis and Distribution Representation in Large Data Sets
Databases.summary: Histograms provide a powerful means of summarizing large data sets by representing their distribution in a compact, binned form. The HistogramTools R package enhances R built-in histogram functionality, offering advanced methods for manipulating and analyzing histograms, especially in large-scale data environments. Key features include the ability to serialize histograms using Protocol Buffers for distributed computing tasks, tools for merging and modifying histograms, and techniques for measuring and visualizing information loss in histogram representations. The package is particularly suited for environments utilizing MapReduce, where efficient storage and data sharing are critical. This paper presents various methods of histogram bin manipulation, distance measures, quantile approximation, and error estimation in cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) derived from histograms. Visualization techniques and efficient storage representations are also discussed alongside applications for large data processing and distributed computing tasks.

Databases.title: Beyond Foreign-Key Connectivity: Semantic Relationship Representation for Relational Deep Learning
Databases.summary:
Relational databases encode information through tables and primary--foreign key constraints. Although recent Relational Deep Learning (RDL) approaches represent these databases as heterogeneous graphs, a foreign-key connection primarily specifies structural connectivity between records. Its semantic interpretation may involve additional information that is not explicitly represented by connectivity alone.
  This paper introduces a conceptual framework for constructing relationship-aware representations from relational databases. The framework distinguishes three complementary aspects: (i) schema-defined relationship semantics, including endpoint types and foreign-key roles; (ii) association entities and explicitly available relationship-level attributes; and (iii) contextual information describing the temporal and structural circumstances of a connection.
  We formulate a Relationship Representation Construction (RRC) protocol that maps relational schema elements and database records to node representations, relationship descriptors, and contextual representations. A key principle of the protocol is semantic ownership: attributes are assigned to records, relationships, or context according to their meaning, rather than merely their physical location in a database table. Ambiguous attributes are not automatically promoted to relationship features.
  The resulting representations can be incorporated into existing relational graph learning architectures through relationship-conditioned message passing. The proposed framework is complementary to recent work on relational message passing, graph transformers, and task-dependent graph construction. We discuss its conceptual foundations, illustrate the construction protocol using a multi-table database, and identify research questions and empirical evaluations required to establish its potential benefits.

Databases.title: VASTRA: Efficient Agentic Top-K Interactive Video Analysis
Databases.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) enable natural language video retrieval, bypassing traditional hand-engineered pipelines. Integrating agentic reasoning frameworks (e.g., ReAct) further advances this paradigm by allowing models to dynamically inspect video content rather than relying on a single visual pass. Applying this pattern naively to video retrieval inherits problems that video systems cannot afford: results vary from run to run under identical conditions, and cost and latency scale with every reasoning step the agent takes rather than with the work the query actually requires. We present VASTRA, an agentic video retrieval system whose execution is dictated by query complexity rather than an open-ended reasoning loop: cheap, reliably answerable queries are ranked directly from pre-ingested summaries, while harder queries trigger targeted verification only where relevance is genuinely uncertain. This keeps control flow external to the model rather than latent in a growing chain of thought, establishing deterministic control flow by construction and end-to-end rank reproducibility under greedy serving. Across 40 benchmark queries, VASTRA exposes explicit presets: VASTRA-Fast runs 12.2x faster (4.2 s vs. 51.2 s) and 10.4x cheaper ($0.0044 vs. $0.0458) than best performing ReAct agent at a 5.0-point mAP reduction, while VASTRA-Max matches peak ReAct agent accuracy (0.653 vs. 0.649 mAP) at comparable latency, trading higher spend ($0.1022 vs. $0.0458) for zero run-to-run variance.

Operating Systems.title: EngineAgent: Agentizing On-Device LLM Inference Engines with Inference Stack Hierarchy Awareness and Hardware Abilities
Operating Systems.summary: Rapidly evolving LLM architectures and heterogeneous mobile hardware make supporting new models in on-device inference engines a recurring and costly system challenge. Each model may require coordinated changes across conversion, graph construction, operators, and hardware backends. Existing coding agents often miss these cross-layer dependencies and struggle to diagnose failures across host--device execution paths. We present EngineAgent, an agentic system for automating on-device LLM model enablement. Its key insight is to separate reusable engine and hardware knowledge from model-specific implementation. Before enablement, EngineAgent constructs a hierarchy-aware engine index that captures engine abstraction layers and cross-layer dependencies, and pre-validates backend-specific build, execution, and debugging workflows using already supported models. For each new model, a builder uses this knowledge to coordinate cross-layer changes, while an auditor checks implementation completeness and drives iterative debugging through device-side validation. Across 12 tasks spanning three mobile LLMs and four engine--backend pairs on CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs, EngineAgent achieves 75% end-to-end success with either of two underlying LLMs, versus 33.3% for the strongest coding-agent baseline. Success requires compilation, on-device execution, and output-logit agreement with reference implementations. EngineAgent also reduces average per-task time and model-API cost relative to baselines using the same underlying LLMs.

Operating Systems.title: Tideway: Phase-Aware Tiered Memory Management for MoE Inference on Consumer Devices
Operating Systems.summary:
Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly becoming a dominant paradigm for AI applications. Recently, there is a growing demand to deploy large-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models locally on consumer PCs to balance data privacy, API costs, and inference efficiency. However, unlike datacenter servers with abundant DRAM, consumer devices are tightly constrained in both GPU VRAM and host RAM, forcing massive MoE weights to spill across VRAM, host RAM, and SSD. Under such spilling, we observe that existing systems fail to fully utilize this memory hierarchy, treating the tiers as independent caches and thrashing in inference.
  We present TIDEWAY, a system for efficient inference of large MoE models on memory-constrained consumer devices. Our core insight is to manage host RAM and GPU VRAM as a unified memory pool. Within this pool, TIDEWAY couples phase-aware memory layouts, which adapt to the distinct access patterns of prefill and decode, with an execution engine that optimizes CUDA Graph execution under expert paging. Our evaluations on representative consumer hardware with frontier MoE models demonstrate that TIDEWAY significantly outperforms state-of-the-art systems. On average, TIDEWAY achieves speedups of 1.97x in end-to-end latency and 2.40x in Time-to-First-Token (TTFT), along with 1.61x higher decode throughput against the fastest baseline.
  Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Afterglow231/Tideway .

Operating Systems.title: MARS: Towards High Goodput and Low KV Thrashing in Agent Serving under GPU Memory Constraints
Operating Systems.summary:
Self-hosted LLM agents offer greater control over sensitive data and model customization while avoiding per-request API fees. However, serving concurrent, multi-turn workflows within limited GPU memory makes it difficult to achieve high workflow-level goodput. In particular, as workflows accumulate context, their reusable key-value (KV) caches can easily outgrow GPU capacity, triggering repeated eviction and recovery, known as KV cache thrashing. This process consumes resources and delays workflow completion. Although existing approaches propose various methods, our motivation study shows that the evaluated baselines still incur substantial thrashing overhead or fail to address the workflow-level goodput issue.
  We present MARS, an agent serving system that coordinates workflow admission and in-engine scheduling to achieve high workflow-level goodput on memory-constrained devices while avoiding KV cache thrashing. Specifically, outside the engine, an admission controller selects root workflows using initial prefix footprint estimates and live KV availability, adapting admissions to memory pressure. Inside, an agent-centric scheduler prioritizes turn completion and coordinates prefill allocation with KV reclamation to reduce disruptive evictions. Across two models and three GPU configurations, MARS achieves 1.59x-7.56x mean end-to-end latency speedups over the fastest baseline. Integrated as the serving backend for OpenCode, Codex, and OpenHands, MARS further improves mean workflow completion time by 1.17x-1.87x.
  Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Afterglow231/MARS_preview .
Operating Systems.comment: 13 pages, 11 figures. Major revision with updated title, system design, and expanded evaluation. Preprint

Performance.title: Measuring Tabular Data Formats Cold: A Replicated Cold-Cache Benchmark of Serialization, Scan, and Index Performance on Real Datasets
Performance.summary: Choosing a file format for tabular data is a routine engineering decision, yet published comparisons often time reads served from the operating-system page cache, use one session, or rely on a single synthetic dataset. This article benchmarks fifteen format and access-path configurations (CSV, JSON Lines, Pickle, Feather, Parquet, ORC, DuckDB, and SQLite, with several access paths) on two real public datasets, New York City taxi trips and United States airline on-time records, at 50,000 to 3 million rows. Every measurement uses an explicitly cold cache, randomized execution order, and three independent sessions (with restarts on the laptop), and is analyzed with bootstrap intervals and Holm-adjusted permutation tests. Parquet answered a filtered aggregation 2.6 to 11 times faster than CSV, while JSON Lines was 10 to 27 times slower. A secondary index made SQLite queries 2.6 to 4.8 times slower on randomly ordered data and helped only on data sorted by the filtered column, at low selectivity. A row filter inside the Parquet reader was significantly faster than a projected scan on flight data from one million rows and on both datasets at three million, and row-group skipping needs several row groups, which the default writer produced only at 3 million rows. A 4 GB Linux host ran out of memory on configurations that a 24 GB laptop completed and reversed some orderings, such as Pickle versus Parquet. Code, derived data, and raw timings are released.
Performance.comment: Submitted to IEEE Open Journal of the Computer Society

Performance.title: Performance Portability Explained: Insights from accelerating ICON microphysics
Performance.summary:
Scientific computing is under increasing pressure to adapt to HPC hardware that is shaped by AI workloads. In these modern ecosystems, extracting reasonable performance without investing major engineering effort is a central issue for domain scientists. Correctness constraints and intricate reference implementations represent further impediments to development. Instead of using a double-precision implementation as a reference, considering the underlying scientific problem directly opens more opportunities for performance improvements when updating and rewriting applications.
  We take seven different portability frameworks---covering pragma-based, DSL, and data-centric approaches---and evaluate them on a microphysics kernel of the ICON climate model. Our performance benchmarks show that each different HPC system benefits from a different combination of optimizations, so we develop the measure of framework expressivity to gauge how easily each framework can customize portable implementations in this way.

Performance.title: WINIC: An Automatic Cycle-Accurate Multi-Platform Microbenchmarking Tool for Instruction Performance Metrics
Performance.summary: Performance models allow developers to gain important insights into the interaction of their code with the hardware that executes it, and enable them to apply target-specific optimizations. To create in-core performance models for out-of-order processors, architecture-specific performance metrics like latency, throughput, and port binding of individual instructions are indispensable. For x86 microarchitectures, there already exist tools to automatically obtain those values; however, the extension of performance modeling tools like the Open Source Architecture Code Analyzer (OSACA) to support further architectures like RISC-V emphasizes the need for a multi-platform microbenchmarking tool. We present WINIC (What I Need Is Cycles), an automatic cross-platform microbenchmarking tool. Unlike previous tools, it can obtain throughput and operand-based latency metrics for most supported instructions of any 64-bit x86, AArch64, and RISC-V microarchitecture without the need for root permissions or extended system control levels. We cover the methodology of microbenchmarking and the approach of WINIC to collect cycle-accurate performance data for assembly instructions. We show that WINIC can be used to automatically obtain a vast number of accurate results and demonstrate for four target microarchitectures that our results match between 71% and 99% of the performance data of instructions obtained by similar tools and documentation. Furthermore, we investigate how operand-based metrics measured by WINIC can be used to improve the in-core performance predictions on selected micro-kernels, exemplarily for the Neoverse V2 microarchitecture.

Performance.title: Scaling Shapley Energy Attribution to Large LLM Batches
Performance.summary:
LLM services have become essential infrastructure for applications such as chat assistants and coding agents. Service providers need to attribute resource consumption to individual requests for purposes such as billing. Among these resources, energy is a key metric for assessing the cost of serving each request. However, serving engines batch requests together, and GPUs report only aggregate energy consumption. Providers typically estimate each request's share in proportion to its token consumption, but this approach can produce substantially unfair estimates. The Shapley value provides a principled solution to fair energy allocation, but computing it directly requires $2^N-1$ GPU runs for $N$ requests, which is infeasible for large batches.
  To address this problem, we propose StepSplit. Across GPU generations, we observe that the energy consumed by each inference step, a forward pass over a batch, consists of a shared energy, largely due to reading model weights, and a request-specific energy. We derive a closed-form Shapley value: each request is charged its own energy plus an equal part of the shared energy of every step in which it participates. A microbenchmark of 2.5-17.8 minutes calibrates both parts of the step energy once per model and GPU configuration. Under static batching, StepSplit uses this closed form in a single pass over the scheduler log. Under continuous batching, removing a request can change how the remaining requests are batched, so StepSplit adds a correction to the closed form, computed by replaying the scheduler on a CPU. We evaluate StepSplit against Shapley values measured using 529,513 GPU runs. Under static batching with batch sizes of 8-256, StepSplit achieves an $L_1$ error of 0.4-4.3%, compared with 13.4-61.3% for token-proportional allocation. Under continuous batching with 8-128 requests, the corresponding errors are 0.5-6.4% and 20.6-71.7%.

Performance.title: Exploiting What NVIDIA Profilers Hide: Fast and Accurate Analytical GPU Performance Modeling
Performance.summary: GPUs have become essential to many fields, including AI and scientific computing. As GPUs grow more complex, the design space of their hardware configurations becomes increasingly large, yet cycle-level simulators remain too slow to explore it. Analytical models make this exploration much faster. However, existing GPU analytical models fall short of accurately predicting performance across hardware configurations, because they re-estimate or scale every stall of a warp on the target configuration. We observe that fixed-latency stalls stay the same across configurations, whereas queueing stalls vary with the pressure on each hardware unit. Based on this observation, we propose ForeSight, a queueing analytical model that reuses the fixed-latency stalls measured on GPU hardware and recomputes the queueing stalls of each hardware unit from its pressure. To provide ForeSight with the counter values of each hardware unit, we build UnitSight, a profiler that recovers these values, which NVIDIA's official profilers hide by aggregating across units. Our evaluation on hardware configurations of nine NVIDIA GPUs shows that ForeSight predicts kernel execution time with a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 8.3%, compared with 14.1% for the best baseline. ForeSight also predicts the end-to-end execution time of LLM inference on vLLM with a MAPE of 2.0%. It runs 49x faster than the cycle-level simulator Accel-Sim and faster than interval-based models such as GCoM. With the aid of ForeSight, we explore configurations derived from the H20 GPU for LLM inference and find one with 1.78x its performance/cost.

Performance.title: OSCAR: Offline Spectral Covariance-Aware Rotation for 2-bit KV Cache Quantization
Performance.summary:
INT2 KV-cache quantization is attractive for long-context LLM serving, yet making it both accurate and practical remains challenging. Data-oblivious rotations such as Hadamard transforms flatten channel outliers, but still degrade sharply at INT2 because they ignore how downstream attention queries the cache. We propose OSCAR, an ultra-low-bit KV-cache quantization method that estimates attention-aware covariance targets offline and uses them to derive fixed per-layer rotations and clipping thresholds. By aligning the quantization basis with the second-moment structures consumed by attention, OSCAR preserves attention fidelity at 2-bit precision. Beyond theoretical analysis under a frozen-error surrogate, we build a serving-ready OSCAR system with fused Triton write and decode kernels that preserve paged KV-cache layouts and prefix caching, integrating into modern serving engines such as SGLang and vLLM.
  We evaluate OSCAR on reasoning and coding benchmarks with generation traces of up to 32K tokens across five tasks. On Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and Qwen3-8B, OSCAR narrows the BF16 accuracy gap to 3.78 and 1.21 points, respectively, where Hadamard-only INT2 collapses, and matches BF16 within run-to-run variance on Qwen3-32B and GLM-4.7 (358B parameters). On RULER-NIAH up to 128K tokens, OSCAR substantially outperforms QuaRot-style INT2 across context lengths. System-wise, OSCAR compresses KV-cache memory by nearly $8\times$, boosts multi-request throughput by up to $7.8\times$ at large batch sizes within the same memory budget, and accelerates batch-size-1 decoding by up to $3.1\times$ over BF16 by cutting KV memory traffic.
Performance.comment: 46 pages, 10 figures. v2 adds matched-baseline comparisons, residual diagnostics, and expanded long-context analysis

Performance.title: UniPipe: Unified Inference Serving and Fine-Tuning for Deadline-Constrained DNN Surrogate Workflows
Performance.summary: DNN surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate scientific workflows that must process high-rate sensor streams in near real time, exemplified by Ptychographic imaging at next-generation X-ray light sources. Such surrogates deliver 100-1000x higher throughput than iterative solvers, enabling faster steering of experiments. To preserve surrogate accuracy during an experiment, as the input distribution evolves, state-of-the-art deployments freeze the pretrained surrogate or run a separate CUDA context that fine-tunes concurrently with serving. However, multi-context concurrency causes significant contention on the GPU, inflating both the mean and the variance of inference latency, triggering deadline misses in workflows where sensor data has to be processed within a hard per-unit deadline. To address this challenge, we propose UniPipe, a single-context system that unifies inference serving and fine-tuning of a DNN surrogate on a single edge GPU. UniPipe is driven by three key insights: both serving and fine-tuning require a forward pass and can be fused into one; the per-sample latency of modern GPUs is non-linear in batch size; and the workload is repetitive across intervals, enabling offline scheduling. Specifically, UniPipe fuses training and inference data in a single forward pass with a selective backward pass on the training subset, and uses a polynomial-time scheduler that exploits the latency curve to compute the batch composition. We evaluate UniPipe on a real-world Ptychographic reconstruction workflow with sensor rates up to 5000 patterns/sec.; UniPipe lowers reconstruction MSE by up to 30% and inference MSE by up to 50% over a pretrained baseline, and reduces the deadline-miss rate by 13%-22% over a multi-context baseline. UniPipe's unified deployment reduces the latency spread from 106% to 57% of the mean, and increases total throughput compared to multi-context baseline.

Performance.title: Reconstructing Fine-grained Memory Reuse Structure in GPU Kernels
Performance.summary: Optimizing GPU data movement requires knowing which instructions access the same data and across which execution scopes reuse occurs. Existing profilers can attribute memory behavior to individual instructions but do not expose the reuse relations among them, while aliasing, dynamic indexing, and runtime parameters prevent static analysis from establishing these relations in general. Cycle-level simulation can reconstruct such relations, but at costs prohibitive for production workloads. We introduce two abstractions for representing this structure: Topological Distance, which labels each dynamic memory access with the smallest execution scope (thread, warp, block, or grid) containing its most recent reuse, and PCDepGraph, which organizes these labels into a PC-level graph of the kernel's memory reuse structure. Defined over logical execution scopes rather than transient hardware state, the representation remains stable across runs and GPU targets while directly indicating the sharing scope that candidate optimization mechanisms must cover. Our tool, cuVein, reconstructs PCDepGraph directly from optimized binaries, without sampling, at generally under 10x overhead. Across HPC and AI workloads on NVIDIA RTX 4090 and H100, optimizations guided by PCDepGraph eliminate up to 90.18% of memory instructions and yield up to 2.84x kernel speedup; reuse-scope distributions remain consistent across platforms, supporting that the representation captures program structure rather than transient hardware behavior.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Medical Image Segmentation: Foundation Model Adaptation versus Task-Specific Training
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Foundation models pretrained on large natural-image collections are increasingly adapted for medical image segmentation, in the expectation that they will replace models trained for each task. Most comparisons, however, use data from the training distribution and a single task-specific baseline whose configuration is rarely justified, and therefore provide limited evidence of performance at new clinical sites. It also remains unclear how much of a foundation model must be adapted, and what determines this. We adapted a foundation model, DINOv2, with strategies ranging from tuning only its bias terms to full fine-tuning, and compared it with U-Nets and ResU-Nets trained from scratch. Experiments covered colonoscopy, breast ultrasound and dermoscopy, with testing on held-out data from the training source and on independent datasets from other institutions. The adapted foundation model generalised better on every external dataset. Within the training distribution, the task-specific models remained competitive when training data were abundant, and delineated boundaries more precisely, while the foundation model more often missed small lesions. Only a small fraction of the foundation model required adaptation, and the capacity needed was determined by the imaging domain rather than by the adaptation method. A widely used polyp test set was also found to duplicate images from another benchmark. Foundation-model adaptation is therefore warranted where models must work across sites, with capacity selected on the target domain.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Multimodal Model Diffing for Feature Discovery and Control
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit strong visual understanding, yet the internal features that cause these behaviors remain difficult to identify, audit, or control. While applicable to post-hoc inspection, hidden states that are decomposed into interpretable feature directions using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) neither readily isolate which features are changed by multimodal training, nor are they directly useful for targeted control. We introduce MMDiff, a multimodal model-diffing framework that trains multimodal SAEs and turns them into feature-level interfaces for discovering and controlling multimodal behavior. MMDiff supports three uses: (i) feature isolation, by diffing a base-LM SAE against its multimodal-adapted counterpart to identify features altered by multimodal training; (ii) task-specific feature detection, via per-token contrastive firing analysis that isolates causal features; and (iii) feature-level control, by causally removing or steering the discovered feature directions. We train multimodal SAEs for three MLLM families, LLaVA-MORE, PaliGemma 2, and InternVL3.5, and evaluate on visual-spatial understanding, multimodal safety, and OCR. MMDiff discovers sparse, causally specific features whose removal selectively degrades target behaviors by an average of 12% on spatial tasks and 17% on OCR, and reduces attack success rate by 24% on multimodal safety attacks, with no impact on VQA performance. Steering these features improves spatial and OCR accuracy by +3.6% and +1.8% on average over a standard single-layer steering baseline. These results show that multimodal SAEs can serve not only as interpretability tools, but as mechanisms for auditing, steering, and controlling MLLMs behavior toward safer and more capable generations.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

Artificial Intelligence.title: Toward Foundation Detection Models via Example-Based Grounding in EM-DETR
Artificial Intelligence.summary: DeepLearning (DL)-based Computer-Aided Diagnostic (CAD) systems have shown great promise in supporting clinicians, but their performance heavily depends on the availability of large, well-annotated datasets. In medical lesion detection, the scarcity of comprehensive, stan dardized annotations and the heterogeneity of existing datasets limit the development of robust foundation models. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to building a multi-domain foundation model for le sion detection by integrating diverse medical image datasets annotated for both anatomical structures and abnormalities. We first propose a student-teacher training strategy to effectively combine datasets with heterogeneous label spaces, mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and im proving feature learning. In addition, building on our previously pro posed example-based EM-DETR framework, we adapt it to jointly learn from multiple domain-specific datasets, enabling fine-grained, example driven detection across modalities. Our model achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) results, with image-level AUC scores exceeding previous SOTA by 1% point on four key findings in CXRs. We achieve a leading mAP50 in CXRs and mammography, surpassing EM-DETR trained on a single dataset by 2-3% points. This approach paves the way for scalable foundation models in medical imaging that leverage heterogeneous data while maintaining robust and generalizable performance.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations
Artificial Intelligence.summary: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery, yet most of them evaluate hypotheses pointwise, testing an empirical claim $h$ only against its complement $\neg h$. When evidence rejects $h$, the agent learns that one explanation is unlikely but not which alternative the evidence supports. To recover that alternative, we introduce Contrastive Discovery, which replaces the single hypothesis with a contrast set, a scientific question paired with mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive competing explanations. Each experiment is scored by how its evidence redistributes belief across the set, and the question is resolved when belief concentrates on one explanation. Because contrast sets change only the unit an agent proposes and scores, an existing agent can use them to re-evaluate evidence it has already collected or to guide its search. Across six domains, $89\%$ of the pointwise candidates with the largest belief shifts are rejections. On the same evidence, contrast sets resolve $73\%$ of these candidates to a specific alternative. When contrast sets guide search, the agent resolves $67\%$ more questions than pointwise surprisal under the same experiment budget. In a blinded study, $38$ human experts chose the same explanation on $78\%$ of resolved questions and on $82\%$ of questions where the pointwise agent rejected its hypothesis and stopped. Together, these results support explicit competing explanations as a way for discovery agents to resolve more scientific questions from the same evidence and validation budget.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 55 pages. Project page: https://codiscovery.ai/contrastive-discovery/

Artificial Intelligence.title: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Deploying LLM-based analytics agents in enterprise settings requires evaluation frameworks that can reliably detect failures across complex, multi-tool workflows. We present a three-phase comparative study of three evaluation frameworks, each representing a distinct evaluation paradigm (trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics), applied to two analytics agents in a controlled research setting using frozen execution traces. Phase 1 quantifies evaluation harness stability through repeated measurements, finding that 97% of configurations meet the stability threshold and that stability patterns are agent-independent. Phase 2 measures known risk detection on 72 ground-truth test cases, where the trace-based framework achieves the best precision-recall balance (F1=0.90) while text-only evaluation matches on recall but generates 5x more false alarms. Phase 3 evaluates unknown risk discovery, uncovering 24 novel failures with zero overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming. Our results demonstrate that (1) the information available to the evaluation harness determines evaluation quality, (2) functional and security evaluation are complementary, and (3) LLM-based evaluation harnesses surface subtle errors that human reviewers miss. We recommend a two-framework strategy: trace-based evaluation for functional assessment and adversarial red-teaming for security validation.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted to KDD 2026, Jeju, Korea. 9 pages, 3 figures

Artificial Intelligence.title: ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Business process automation runs the same Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) again and again on new inputs. Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow an SOP written in natural language, but they call an LLM to choose every step of every run, which adds latency and cost at scale. We present ReTrace, which turns an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow in which code, not an LLM, selects the next step. The agent's reasoning, the explanation it writes with each tool call, often states why it took an action; the tool calls alone do not. ReTrace extracts the condition behind each step, merges these conditions across runs into a compact rule document, and generates an executable workflow from it. Only this last stage depends on the platform, so rule documents can be compiled for different orchestration platforms. On $79$ procedures from our production platform, ReTrace workflows reach $93.8\%$ completion, against $96.8\%$ for the agent, at $24\%$ lower cost per task. On $τ^2$-Bench, they reach $75.8\%$ task success (agent: $80.6\%$) and run in $1.3$s instead of $170$s; three rounds of repair on training failures lift $k{=}2$ workflows from $66.7\%$ to $81.2\%$. On eight SOP-Bench procedures, ReTrace without repair trails few-shot generation ($80.6\%$ vs. $83.6\%$), but repair from labeled training failures lifts it to $87.8\%$ at $0.40$s per task, compared to $85.5\%$ in $46.6$s for the agent.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Re-Search: Dissecting LLM Ideation Through a Two-Player Questioning Game
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Research ideation is iterative: researchers refine their ideas step by step based on feedback. Yet existing evaluations obscure this search process, making it difficult to understand how LLMs explore the space of research ideas and what limits their progress. We introduce Re-Search, which adapts the format of Twenty Questions to research ideation: given only the research problem of a published paper, a model must rediscover the paper's core idea by asking yes-or-no questions. Built from 200 ICML 2026 papers, Re-Search tracks how a model's idea evolves as it asks questions and receives binary oracle feedback, isolating ideation from execution. Across six recent LLMs, nearly all progress happens within the first 30 of 100 questions, which largely decide how the game ends; after that, most models plateau. Through controlled interventions on the candidate questions and the hypothesis space, we find that the bottleneck is generation, not judgment: models recognize a good idea or a good question when one is offered, but often cannot produce it on their own. We further analyze the ideation traces and find that models fail by either over-exploiting one direction or over-exploring too many. These findings point to concrete design principles for autoresearch systems: since models can judge candidates they cannot produce, enriching the search with externally sourced ideas and questions may be more effective than improving any single model's generation ability.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Beyond the Mean Gap: What Transferred-Angle QAOA Retains on a Superconducting Processor
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Hardware executions of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) are often validated by comparing the device's mean cost with a simulation, a check that can miss what matters for optimization. Under global depolarization, the mean normalized gap and the floor-corrected probability of every set of bitstrings, the optimum included, retain the same fraction of their noiseless improvement over uniform sampling. We test this prediction with depth-2, transferred-angle QAOA circuits for binary subproblems of an alternating-direction decomposition on the IBM Heron processor \texttt{ibm\_marrakesh}, with and without dynamical decoupling and twirling. At 12 qubits, the main-family circuits retained 29\% to 46\% of their mean-gap improvement but only 5\% to 15\% of their probability of the optimum, lower on at least nine of ten instances per run. Near-optimal bitstrings were lost about as much as the optimum, whereas the avoidance of poor bitstrings was retained best. In the first submission, a device-matched noise model reproduced the pattern but overestimated the retention of the optimum five- to eightfold. On a rugged planted family, the device found the optimum in 62\% of 768-shot blocks (noiseless: 98\%), within the range of local heuristics. Validations of optimization circuits should report retention of the optimum and of near-optimal sets.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Learning to Reason from Reference Samples Alone: Reinforced Adversarial Learning for Modern LLM Post-Training
Artificial Intelligence.summary: In many settings where LLM post-training is desirable, high-quality answers are recognizable but difficult to score with explicit rewards. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is limited to tasks where an explicit correctness signal is available. Prior adversarial approaches to training reasoning LLMs either complement verifiable rewards with co-trained critics or require reference reasoning traces. We ask whether a co-trained LLM judge can turn reference answers alone into the sole reward for on-policy post-training of reasoning LLMs. We call this method Reinforced Adversarial Learning (RAL). We first validate RAL on three verifiable tasks (integer multiplication, code-based arithmetic-expression synthesis, and SMILES-to-formula translation), using the verifiers only for evaluation. With sufficiently capable judges and enough training, RAL matches direct RLVR. We then apply RAL to scientific abstract generation in two settings. In the first setting, RAL guides the generator to produce abstracts in the scientific domain of the reference abstracts, even though the prompt leaves that domain unspecified. In the second setting, we generate abstracts for U.S. National Institutes of Health grant proposals conditioned on the grant title. Human scientists and an ensemble of LLM judges find our generations harder to distinguish from real abstracts than those of frontier-LLM baselines. These results suggest a path toward post-training reasoning models in scientific and other high-value domains, where increasingly capable judges infer hard-to-specify reward functions from example answers.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 31 pages, 6 figures, 10 tables, including references and appendices

Artificial Intelligence.title: Diff-Instruct with Diffused Reward: Towards Principled One-step Generator RL
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Recent advances in one-step text-to-image generation have enabled real-time synthesis with remarkable efficiency and quality. Previous reinforcement learning methods for one-step generators combine image-space reward optimization with diffusion noisy-space distribution matching. This paradigm brings challenges due to a mismatch between terminal reward optimization and the underlying generative dynamics. As a result, optimization tends to exploit stochastic degrees of freedom, often improving reward at the expense of image fidelity. To address this issue, we propose Diff-Instruct with Diffused Reward (DIDR), a data-free trajectory-level alignment framework derived from Integral KL minimization. DIDR propagates the RLHF-optimal reward-tilted clean-image distribution across all noise levels along the diffusion trajectory. We show that this objective admits the same minimizer as clean-image RLHF, while naturally inducing the Diffused Reward Score (DRS), which acts as a reward-driven correction to the reference score function. To make this practical, we further introduce the Diffused Reward Proxy (DRP), an efficient estimator of DRS based on differentiable short-step denoising. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DIDR consistently Pareto-dominates existing one-step SDXL baselines. Moreover, when transferred to a 6B DiT backbone (Z-Image), DIDR surpasses its 50-step teacher in preference alignment while requiring only a single generation step. Code: https://github.com/Junyi-W/DIDR
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 33 pages. Updated manuscript and author information

Artificial Intelligence.title: SupplyNetPy: An Open-Source Python Library for High-Fidelity Modeling and Simulation of Arbitrary Supply Chain and Inventory Networks
Artificial Intelligence.summary: This paper introduces SupplyNetPy, an open-source, well-documented Python library for modeling and discrete-event simulation of supply chain networks with arbitrary multi-echelon structures. It supports multiple replenishment policies, perishable inventory, node disruptions, and stochastic demand and lead times. All components are extensible via inheritance. Users describe a supply chain as a graph with node and link attributes, while the library handles simulation, providing logs and extensive node and network level performance reports. This paper presents the motivation, design, key features, and architecture of SupplyNetPy, along with detailed validation results (against analytical benchmarks, a commercial tool, and a published case study). A key motivation behind SupplyNetPy's development is programmatic generation and simulation of complex models, enabling design-space exploration, what-if analysis, training data generation, and supply chain digital twins.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted to the Winter Simulation Conference 2026

Artificial Intelligence.title: From AGI to ASI
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Over the last decade, building human-level artificial general intelligence has moved from far-fetched speculation to being a concrete next-decade target for many of the largest AI organizations. Achieving this goal would have profound and far-reaching impacts on human society, which raises many complex questions for the decade ahead. This report investigates how AI itself might continue to develop in a post-AGI world along the continuum of machine intelligence. The endpoint of this continuum, Universal AI, is theoretically well understood, which provides some formal grounding for the main focus of this report: the transition from human-level AGI to artificial general superintelligence, which can intuitively be understood as a system that is more intelligent and cognitively capable than large organizations of humans. After characterizing ASI, the report discusses four potential pathways from AGI to ASI: scaling AGI, AI paradigm shifts, ASI emerging from large-scale multi-agent collectives, and recursive improvement. The report then discusses possible frictions and bottlenecks along these pathways. Determining whether the impact of these frictions will be negligible or substantial raises a number of concrete open research questions. While large uncertainties for predicting ASI progress remain, it cannot be ruled out that AI progress might continue to accelerate over the next years. This would imply that the image of a single transformative step change, caused by the introduction of human-level AGI into our society, could be inaccurate. More apt might be the prospect of a series of transformative societal changes caused by AI-enabled progress and breakthroughs across many areas of science and technology. Preparing for this prospect requires a massively interdisciplinary endeavor of global scope and interest.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: v3: minor fixes, overhaul of RSI mechanisms, and addition cognitive industrialization

Artificial Intelligence.title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge
Artificial Intelligence.summary: We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10. The core of the solution is a single vision-language-action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution, which is based on $π_{0.5}$. On the 50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392. Our main conclusion from 2025 was that the model was undertrained, so most of the 2026 work went into training the model for longer, optimizing some training parameters, making each training step slightly faster and reducing the gradient noise: a migration from 50 to 100 tasks (semantic stages built from the demonstrations' skill annotations, task and stage embeddings of new tasks warm-started from similar old ones, and a 21-dimensional action space matching the teleoperation controls); variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching with a simple noise-vs-compute model that picks the number of action-expert samples per observation without ablations; and a 200k-step training run, about one pass over the 211M frames of the demonstrations. A cloud evaluation infrastructure keeps a shared record with provenance, episode diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators on one GPU together faster than real time. On top of the learned policy, 14 tasks are routed to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent that controls the robot through observation and motion tools, starting every episode from a frozen copy of its own practice session on training instances. Across these 14 tasks, Astra's mean Q is 0.639, against 0.108 for the learned policy. The public submission included only part of the Astra results and scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Two Communities, One Problem: Branch-and-Bound vs. A* for Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Branch-and-Bound (B&B) and $A^*$ are popular exact search methods originating from Operations Research and Artificial Intelligence, respectively. Although the two methods share fundamental search principles, their different ways of exploring the search space can lead to substantially different computational performance.
